passages.title: Received gifts lead into a prayer for understanding rather than a claim to rank
passages.summary: The letter opens in Paul’s name to the saints at Ephesus. It blesses God for choosing them in Christ before the world’s foundation. In Christ they have redemption through his blood and forgiveness. God plans to sum up all things in Christ. They were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, a pledge of their inheritance. Paul has heard of their faith and love and gives thanks. He prays that they will know their hope and God’s power. That power raised Christ and made him head over all things.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.

lds.text: Doctrine and Covenants 27:13 also speaks of the fulness of times (verse 10). Why does the opening blessing lead into a prayer for understanding?

contextNote.title: Received gifts lead into a prayer for understanding rather than a claim to rank
contextNote.text: Verses 3–14 list gifts already given: choosing, redemption, an inheritance, the Spirit. The prayer in verses 17–19 asks for nothing new to be added. It asks that they see what they have. Verse 18 pictures the heart with eyes that need light. Three things are to be known. The verse names two: the hope of his calling and his rich inheritance. Verse 19 names the third: the greatness of his power toward believers.

passages.title: Former outsiders become members of one household through the removal of hostility
passages.summary: Paul says the readers were dead in trespasses and followed this world’s course. God, rich in mercy, made them alive with Christ. They are saved by grace through faith, so no one can boast. They are created for good works. As Gentiles they were once far from Israel’s covenants and without hope. Christ’s blood brought them near. He broke down the dividing wall and made the two into one new man. Now they are built together into a holy temple.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson applies the building image to Christ, apostles, and prophets. How do good works follow received grace rather than supply a reason to boast?

contextNote.title: Former outsiders become members of one household through the removal of hostility
contextNote.text: Verse 12 lists what the Gentile readers lacked. They were apart from Christ, shut out of Israel, strangers to the covenants. Verse 14 says Christ broke down the wall of hostility. Verse 19 restates their position with the same kind of words. They are no longer strangers and foreigners. They are fellow citizens and members of God’s household. Verse 20 turns household into house, built on the apostles and prophets.

passages.title: The prisoner's task serves shared inheritance and leads into prayer for strength
passages.summary: Paul calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus for the Gentiles. A mystery was made known to him by revelation. Earlier generations did not know it as it is now revealed. The Gentiles are fellow heirs and members of the same body. Paul, the least of all saints, was given grace to announce Christ’s riches. He asks them not to lose heart over his troubles. He kneels and prays that they be strengthened and rooted in love. He ends with praise to God, who can do far more than they ask.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.

lds.text: Why does the speaker ask the hearers not to lose heart over his troubles?

contextNote.title: The prisoner's task serves shared inheritance and leads into prayer for strength
contextNote.text: Verse 3 speaks of a mystery made known by revelation. Verse 5 says other generations did not know it as now. Verse 6 states its content in three words that begin “fellow.” The Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members, and fellow partakers of the promise. Each word gives them a full share with Israel’s believers. The means is named at the end: through the good news. Verse 1 shows the cost to Paul: he is a prisoner for these Gentiles.

passages.title: One body needs different gifts and conduct that allows its members to grow
passages.summary: Paul, a prisoner, urges them to walk worthy of their calling. He names one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, and one God. Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds, and teachers to build up the body. The body is to grow up into Christ, its head. They must no longer walk as the Gentiles do. They are to put off the old man and put on the new. He gives commands about lying, anger, stealing, and speech. They are to forgive each other as God forgave them.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches that different responsibilities strengthen and unify the Church. How does truthful speech protect members of the same body?

contextNote.title: One body needs different gifts and conduct that allows its members to grow
contextNote.text: Verses 22–24 speak of putting off the old man and putting on the new. Verse 25 gives the first plain case, and it starts with “therefore.” They are to put away falsehood and speak truth with a neighbor. The reason is not a rule about lying in general. It is that “we are members of one another.” The phrase recalls the body in verse 16, where each part supplies. A lie between members harms the body both belong to.

passages.title: Shared submission leads into unequal household roles measured against Christ's self-giving love
passages.summary: Paul tells them to imitate God and walk in love, as Christ loved them. Sexual immorality, greed, and coarse talk should not be named among them. They were once darkness and are now light in the Lord. They should use the time wisely and be filled with the Spirit. They should sing, give thanks, and submit to one another. Wives are told to submit to their husbands as to the Lord. Husbands are told to love their wives as Christ loved the assembly. Paul quotes Genesis on two becoming one flesh and calls it a great mystery.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches family care through the Savior's example. How does Christ's self-giving love shape the command to husbands?

contextNote.title: Shared submission leads into unequal household roles measured against Christ's self-giving love
contextNote.text: Verse 21 tells all of them to submit to one another. Verses 22–24 then address wives, and verses 25–33 address husbands at greater length. Verse 25 gives the husband’s part a measure: love as Christ loved the assembly. That love is defined by an act: he “gave himself up for her.” Verse 28 adds a second measure: husbands should love wives as their own bodies. Verse 29 says no one hates his own flesh but feeds it.

passages.title: Household commands lead into shared resistance supported by peace and prayer
passages.summary: Children are told to obey their parents, and fathers not to provoke their children. Servants are told to obey their masters as serving Christ. Masters are told to stop threatening, for they have the same Master in heaven. Paul then tells all to be strong in the Lord. They are to put on the whole armor of God. He names truth as a belt, faith as a shield, and the Spirit’s sword. They are to pray at all times. He asks prayer for himself, an ambassador in chains, and sends Tychicus.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches care for children and protection through the armor of God. Why does the armor passage lead into prayer for the imprisoned speaker?

contextNote.title: Household commands lead into shared resistance supported by peace and prayer
contextNote.text: Verse 11 says to put on armor against the devil’s schemes. Verse 12 explains who the fight is against, and who it is not. It is not against flesh and blood. That excludes human opponents, even the ones who chained Paul (verse 20). The enemies named are powers, rulers of darkness, and spiritual forces. The armor fits that fight: truth, righteousness, peace, faith, and God’s word. Verse 18 adds prayer for all the saints.

ancientRoads.title: Appian Way
ancientRoads.summary: The Appian Way joined Rome with Capua and the port of Brundisium. Rome began it in 312 BCE.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 28:15 says believers met Paul at the Market of Appius and Three Taverns. Both were stops on this road south of Rome.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The road’s course is well known. The line joins its main towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Egnatia
ancientRoads.summary: Rome built this road across Macedonia in the second century BCE. It ran from the Adriatic coast to Thessalonica and on to Byzantium.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 16:11–17:1 takes Paul through Neapolis, Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia, and Thessalonica. The encyclopedia article places that trip on this road.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones mark the road as far as the edge of Thrace. The line joins known towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Sebaste
ancientRoads.summary: Rome finished this army road in 6 BCE. It climbed from Perga on the coast to Antioch of Pisidia. A branch reached Iconium and Lystra.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 13:14 takes Paul from Perga to Antioch of Pisidia. He may have used this road, but Acts does not say.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones fix parts of the road. The line between the towns is simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Cilician Gates pass
ancientRoads.summary: This pass crosses the Taurus Mountains north of Tarsus. It joins the plain of Cilicia with the high plateau.
ancientRoads.detail: Armies and traders used the pass for a very long time. Acts 15:41 sends Paul through Cilicia but does not name the pass.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass is certain. The line beyond it is a broad guide.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

regions.name: Judea · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome removed Herod’s son Archelaus in 6 CE and made Judea a province. Its governor lived at Caesarea on the coast.
regions.detail: Governors Felix and Festus hold Paul at Caesarea (Acts 23–26). Acts 12 names an earlier ruler King Herod; historians call him Agrippa I.
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins Judea, Samaria, and Idumea. The province grew after 44 CE.

regions.name: Syria · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Syria a province in 64 BCE. It bordered the lands of Herod’s family on the north.
regions.detail: Believers are first called Christians at Antioch in Syria (Acts 11:26). Antioch sends out Barnabas and Saul in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Cilicia · approximate
regions.summary: Cilicia lay on the south coast of Asia Minor. Rome took it in 64 BCE.
regions.detail: Paul comes from Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts 21:39). He passes through Syria and Cilicia in Acts 15:41.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows the eastern plain around Tarsus only.

regions.name: Cyprus · Roman province
regions.summary: Cyprus was a Roman province under a proconsul. Paphos was its capital.
regions.detail: Barnabas comes from Cyprus (Acts 4:36). He and Saul cross the island from Salamis to Paphos in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape follows the modern coast of the island.

regions.name: Galatia · Roman province
regions.summary: Augustus made Galatia a province in 25 BCE. Ancyra was its capital.
regions.detail: Paul writes to the assemblies of Galatia. Acts 13–14 places him at Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Pamphylia on the south coast belonged to Galatia for a time.

regions.name: Asia · Roman province
regions.summary: Asia was a rich Roman province in western Asia Minor. A proconsul governed it.
regions.detail: Paul teaches in Ephesus for two years (Acts 19:10). Revelation 1–3 writes to seven assemblies in Asia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Bithynia and Pontus · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome joined Bithynia and Pontus into one province on the Black Sea coast.
regions.detail: The Spirit keeps Paul from entering Bithynia (Acts 16:7). First Peter greets believers in Pontus and Bithynia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the coast lands.

regions.name: Cappadocia · Roman province
regions.summary: Cappadocia became a Roman province in 17 CE. Its capital was a city named Caesarea.
regions.detail: People from Cappadocia hear Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). First Peter 1:1 greets believers there.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. This Caesarea is not the port in Judea.

regions.name: Macedonia · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Macedonia a province in 146 BCE. The Via Egnatia crossed it from west to east.
regions.detail: A vision calls Paul to Macedonia (Acts 16:9). He teaches in Philippi, Thessalonica, and Beroea.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It includes Thessaly and Epirus, which the province held.

regions.name: Achaia · Roman province
regions.summary: Achaia covered southern Greece. Augustus made it a province apart from Macedonia.
regions.detail: Paul speaks in Athens and stays in Corinth (Acts 17–18). Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, hears a charge against him.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. The province’s islands are not marked.

regions.name: Crete · part of a Roman province
regions.summary: Rome governed Crete together with Cyrenaica in North Africa.
regions.detail: Paul’s ship shelters along Crete in Acts 27. Paul leaves Titus in Crete to appoint elders (Titus 1:5).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the island. Cyrenaica is not marked.

regions.name: Italy
regions.summary: Italy was the home region of Rome. It had a special status among Roman lands.
regions.detail: Paul lands at Puteoli and goes on to Rome (Acts 28). Hebrews 13:24 sends greetings from the Italians.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the peninsula.

guides.title: Ephesians: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Former outsiders become members of one household through the removal of hostility
steps.text: Verse 12 lists what the Gentile readers lacked. They were apart from Christ, shut out of Israel, strangers to the covenants. Verse 14 says Christ broke down the wall of hostility. Verse 19 restates their position with the same kind of words. They are no longer strangers and foreigners. They are fellow citizens and members of God’s household. Verse 20 turns household into house, built on the apostles and prophets.

steps.title: One body needs different gifts and conduct that allows its members to grow
steps.text: Verses 22–24 speak of putting off the old man and putting on the new. Verse 25 gives the first plain case, and it starts with “therefore.” They are to put away falsehood and speak truth with a neighbor. The reason is not a rule about lying in general. It is that “we are members of one another.” The phrase recalls the body in verse 16, where each part supplies. A lie between members harms the body both belong to.

steps.title: Shared submission leads into unequal household roles measured against Christ's self-giving love
steps.text: Verse 21 tells all of them to submit to one another. Verses 22–24 then address wives, and verses 25–33 address husbands at greater length. Verse 25 gives the husband’s part a measure: love as Christ loved the assembly. That love is defined by an act: he “gave himself up for her.” Verse 28 adds a second measure: husbands should love wives as their own bodies. Verse 29 says no one hates his own flesh but feeds it.

steps.title: Household commands lead into shared resistance supported by peace and prayer
steps.text: Verse 11 says to put on armor against the devil’s schemes. Verse 12 explains who the fight is against, and who it is not. It is not against flesh and blood. That excludes human opponents, even the ones who chained Paul (verse 20). The enemies named are powers, rulers of darkness, and spiritual forces. The armor fits that fight: truth, righteousness, peace, faith, and God’s word. Verse 18 adds prayer for all the saints.

chapterMaps.note: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.
chapterMaps.narrative: The letter opens in Paul’s name to the saints at Ephesus. It blesses God for choosing them in Christ before the world’s foundation. In Christ they have redemption through his blood and forgiveness. God plans to sum up all things in Christ. They were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, a pledge of their inheritance. Paul has heard of their faith and love and gives thanks. He prays that they will know their hope and God’s power. That power raised Christ and made him head over all things.

chapterMaps.note: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul says the readers were dead in trespasses and followed this world’s course. God, rich in mercy, made them alive with Christ. They are saved by grace through faith, so no one can boast. They are created for good works. As Gentiles they were once far from Israel’s covenants and without hope. Christ’s blood brought them near. He broke down the dividing wall and made the two into one new man. Now they are built together into a holy temple.
chapterMaps.limits: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.

chapterMaps.note: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus for the Gentiles. A mystery was made known to him by revelation. Earlier generations did not know it as it is now revealed. The Gentiles are fellow heirs and members of the same body. Paul, the least of all saints, was given grace to announce Christ’s riches. He asks them not to lose heart over his troubles. He kneels and prays that they be strengthened and rooted in love. He ends with praise to God, who can do far more than they ask.
chapterMaps.limits: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.

chapterMaps.note: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul, a prisoner, urges them to walk worthy of their calling. He names one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, and one God. Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds, and teachers to build up the body. The body is to grow up into Christ, its head. They must no longer walk as the Gentiles do. They are to put off the old man and put on the new. He gives commands about lying, anger, stealing, and speech. They are to forgive each other as God forgave them.
chapterMaps.limits: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.

chapterMaps.note: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul tells them to imitate God and walk in love, as Christ loved them. Sexual immorality, greed, and coarse talk should not be named among them. They were once darkness and are now light in the Lord. They should use the time wisely and be filled with the Spirit. They should sing, give thanks, and submit to one another. Wives are told to submit to their husbands as to the Lord. Husbands are told to love their wives as Christ loved the assembly. Paul quotes Genesis on two becoming one flesh and calls it a great mystery.

chapterMaps.note: The map marks Ephesus as one city point. It shows no prison or house.
chapterMaps.narrative: Children are told to obey their parents, and fathers not to provoke their children. Servants are told to obey their masters as serving Christ. Masters are told to stop threatening, for they have the same Master in heaven. Paul then tells all to be strong in the Lord. They are to put on the whole armor of God. He names truth as a belt, faith as a shield, and the Spirit’s sword. They are to pray at all times. He asks prayer for himself, an ambassador in chains, and sends Tychicus.
